firstMessage.rawMarkdown:
I submitted "Gemma Reads the Decision. Does the Code Follow?" to the paper track. It started with a small local coding pilot: could Gemma use a saved project decision to finish a feature?

With a pointer and an explicit read instruction, Gemma 4 E2B read the decision file in 18/18 episodes. Without them, it read it in 0/18. Working feature completion was 1/18 in both conditions. The original decision grader also admitted false positives, so reading the file did not establish that the decision reached working code.

A later, separately frozen study tested 12 runnable Python tasks, with three repetitions per condition. Fully passing patches were:

- Request only: 3/36
- Concise handover supplying the decision: 11/36
- Broader evidence packet supplying the same decision: 12/36

The supplied decision helped in this task set. The one-pass difference between the two informative packages does not establish a benefit for broader history. Five of the 12 tasks were never solved in any condition.

These are small, author-written tasks on one model and workstation. Repetitions share tasks, and the results are descriptive. The public release contains the paper only; the companion evidence dataset remains private, so readers cannot replay the results from the repository.

Submitted writeup:
https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/gemma-4-developer-agent-paper/writeups/new-writeup-1793803326040

Readable paper and PDF:
https://github.com/Morkeeth/gemma-decision-paper

For others testing project history in coding agents: how do you check whether a recovered decision actually reached the patch, while preserving unrelated behavior? I would be interested in task designs or grader checks that catch that gap.
